titlePl: Matura PR: Świat przyrody — 180 haseł do gier LingoSpark
titleEn: Matura Extended: Nature — 180 terms for LingoSpark games
blurbPl: Dział Świat przyrody na maturę rozszerzoną: klimat, ekosystemy, klęski żywiołowe i ochrona środowiska. Fiszki ENG–PL.
blurbEn: Extended Matura Natural world module: climate, ecosystems, natural disasters and environmental protection. ENG–PL flashcards.

items.definitionEn: a period of unusually hot weather lasting several days
items.example: A long heatwave dried up rivers and reservoirs across the country.

items.definitionEn: a long period with far too little rain
items.example: Crops failed after a summer of drought in the south.

items.definitionEn: rain, snow, sleet or hail that falls from the sky
items.example: Annual precipitation is much higher in the mountains than on the coast.

items.definitionEn: the amount of water vapour in the air
items.example: High humidity makes hot weather even harder to bear.

items.definitionEn: extremely heavy rain that falls very fast
items.example: Torrential rain flooded the underpass within minutes.

items.definitionEn: a sudden, heavy fall of rain
items.example: We waited under a bus shelter until the downpour stopped.

items.definitionPl: pogoda nietypowa jak na porę roku
items.definitionEn: weather that is unusual for that time of year
items.example: Unseasonable weather in April brought snow to the lowlands.

items.definitionEn: a winter that is warmer than usual
items.example: A mild winter meant that some plants never fully went dormant.

items.definitionEn: a climate that is neither extremely hot nor extremely cold
items.example: Poland has a temperate climate with four distinct seasons.

items.definitionEn: a climate with very little rainfall
items.example: Few crops can grow without irrigation in an arid climate.

items.definitionEn: the distinctive climate of a small area
items.example: The valley has a warmer microclimate than the surrounding hills.

items.definitionEn: the wind that most often blows in a particular region
items.example: The prevailing wind from the west brings wet weather from the Atlantic.

items.definitionEn: the weight of the air pressing down on the Earth
items.example: Falling atmospheric pressure often means that a storm is approaching.

items.definitionEn: long-term shifts in temperature and weather patterns, largely caused by human activity
items.example: Scientists warn that climate change will make droughts more frequent.

items.definitionEn: the rise in the Earth's average temperature
items.example: Global warming is melting ice in the polar regions.

items.definitionEn: the way certain gases trap heat in the atmosphere
items.example: The greenhouse effect is essential for life, but extra gases make it dangerously strong.

items.definitionEn: a gas such as carbon dioxide that traps heat in the atmosphere
items.example: Methane is a greenhouse gas far more potent than carbon dioxide in the short term.

items.definitionEn: a greenhouse gas produced by burning fossil fuels and by breathing
items.example: Power stations release huge amounts of carbon dioxide into the air.

items.definitionEn: the amount of greenhouse gas produced by a person, product or activity
items.example: Flying frequently increases your carbon footprint more than taking the train.

items.definitionEn: the amount of land and resources needed to support a lifestyle
items.example: A diet rich in meat has a larger ecological footprint than a plant-based one.

items.definitionEn: a layer of gas in the upper atmosphere that blocks harmful ultraviolet rays
items.example: Chemicals once used in fridges damaged the ozone layer.

items.definitionEn: the thinning of the ozone layer caused by certain chemicals
items.example: International bans on CFCs have slowed ozone depletion.

items.definitionEn: the urgent, large-scale threat posed by rapid climate change
items.example: Young people marched to demand action on the climate crisis.

items.definitionEn: weather that is unusually severe, such as violent storms or record heat
items.example: Insurance costs are rising because of more extreme weather.

items.definitionEn: the increase in the height of the world's oceans
items.example: Low-lying islands are already threatened by sea-level rise.

items.definitionEn: a thick layer of ice covering a large area, especially at the poles
items.example: The polar ice cap has shrunk dramatically in recent decades.

items.definitionEn: a huge, slow-moving mass of ice in mountains or polar regions
items.example: Hikers can still see a glacier in the Tatras, but it is retreating.

items.definitionEn: ground that stays frozen all year in polar regions
items.example: Roads built on permafrost crack when the ice beneath them thaws.

items.definitionEn: the process by which fertile land becomes dry and desert-like
items.example: Overgrazing can speed up desertification in dry regions.

items.definitionEn: a seasonal wind that brings heavy rain, especially in South Asia
items.example: The monsoon is vital for rice harvests in the region.

items.definitionEn: dirty air caused by smoke, exhaust fumes and fog mixing
items.example: Winter smog in the city often exceeds safe limits.

items.definitionEn: rain made acidic by pollution, which damages forests and lakes
items.example: Acid rain damaged spruce forests in the mountains in the 1980s.

items.definitionEn: the edge of the land where it meets the sea
items.example: Erosion is changing the coastline by several metres a year.

items.definitionEn: land that is covered with water for much of the year
items.example: The wetland is a stopover for thousands of migrating birds.

items.definitionEn: low, wet land that is often flooded
items.example: Draining marshland destroyed the habitat of rare frogs.

items.definitionEn: a wet area of land made of decaying plants, used as a carbon store
items.example: Digging up a peat bog releases carbon that was locked away for centuries.

items.definitionEn: the wide tidal mouth of a river where it meets the sea
items.example: Wading birds feed on the mudflats of the estuary at low tide.

items.definitionEn: flat land formed where a river splits into branches before the sea
items.example: The river delta is fertile but vulnerable to flooding.

items.definitionEn: a smaller river that flows into a larger one
items.example: Pollution in a tributary can contaminate the whole river system.

items.definitionEn: flat land beside a river that floods in heavy rain
items.example: Building on a floodplain puts homes at unnecessary risk.

items.definitionEn: water stored under the ground in soil and rock
items.example: Intensive farming can pollute groundwater with fertilisers.

items.definitionEn: an underground layer of rock that holds water
items.example: The city draws drinking water from a deep aquifer.

items.definitionEn: soil that is rich in nutrients and good for growing crops
items.example: The valley is famous for its fertile soil and vegetable farms.

items.definitionEn: the wearing away of topsoil by wind or water
items.example: Bare fields after harvest are especially prone to soil erosion.

items.definitionEn: the slow breaking down of rock by weather, water or plants
items.example: Frost weathering has split the cliff face into loose slabs.

items.definitionEn: an underwater structure built by corals, rich in marine life
items.example: Tourists were banned from the coral reef to let it recover.

items.definitionEn: trees that grow in salty coastal water and protect the shore
items.example: A mangrove forest shields the village from storm surges.

items.definitionEn: a cold, treeless region with a short growing season
items.example: Only mosses and low shrubs survive on the tundra.

items.definitionEn: a grassy plain with scattered trees in a hot climate
items.example: Herds of antelope graze on the African savannah.

items.definitionEn: land covered with trees, often smaller than a forest
items.example: Ancient woodland supports more species than a newly planted forest.

items.definitionEn: the upper layer of leaves and branches in a forest
items.example: Birds nest high in the forest canopy, out of reach of foxes.

items.definitionEn: bushes and plants growing beneath the trees
items.example: Deer disappeared into the undergrowth at the first sound of voices.

items.definitionEn: a piece of land almost surrounded by water
items.example: The Hel peninsula is a narrow strip of land in the Baltic.

items.definitionEn: a group of islands
items.example: The archipelago is a national park with strict landing rules.

items.definitionEn: a large area of high, fairly flat land
items.example: Villages on the plateau have cooler summers than the coast.

items.definitionEn: the physical features of an area of land
items.example: Rescue teams struggled because the terrain was steep and rocky.

items.definitionEn: a type of animal or plant at serious risk of dying out
items.example: The lynx is an endangered species in this part of Europe.

items.definitionEn: the natural environment where a plant or animal lives
items.example: Wetland drainage has destroyed the habitat of many wading birds.

items.definitionEn: an animal that hunts and kills other animals for food
items.example: The wolf is a predator that keeps deer numbers in check.

items.definitionEn: an animal that is hunted by another animal
items.example: Owls hunt small mammals, which are their main prey.

items.definitionEn: a series of living things in which each is eaten by the next
items.example: If insects disappear, the whole food chain above them is at risk.

items.definitionEn: a community of living things and their physical environment
items.example: A coral reef is a fragile ecosystem that is easily damaged.

items.definitionEn: the variety of plant and animal species in an area
items.example: Tropical rainforests contain more biodiversity than any other land habitat.

items.definitionEn: the plants of a particular region or period
items.example: The alpine flora includes many species found nowhere else.

items.definitionEn: the animals of a particular region or period
items.example: The island's fauna has evolved in isolation for millions of years.

items.definitionEn: a warm-blooded animal that feeds its young on milk
items.example: A bat is the only mammal that can truly fly.

items.definitionEn: an animal such as a frog that lives both in water and on land
items.example: The pond is an important breeding site for every local amphibian.

items.definitionEn: a cold-blooded animal such as a snake, lizard or turtle
items.example: The sand lizard is a reptile that needs sunny, dry slopes.

items.definitionEn: an animal without a backbone, such as an insect or worm
items.example: Soil health depends on invertebrate species that break down dead plants.

items.definitionEn: an animal, often an insect, that carries pollen from one flower to another
items.example: The bee is the most important pollinator of fruit trees.

items.definitionEn: an animal that feeds on dead animals or waste
items.example: The vulture is a scavenger that helps keep the savannah clean.

items.definitionEn: an animal that eats only plants
items.example: An elephant is a herbivore that can strip bark from trees.

items.definitionEn: an animal that eats other animals
items.example: The lynx is a carnivore that hunts mainly deer.

items.definitionEn: a predator at the top of the food chain, with no natural enemies
items.example: The shark is an apex predator in many ocean ecosystems.

items.definitionEn: a species whose presence keeps a whole ecosystem in balance
items.example: Beavers are a keystone species because their dams create wetlands.

items.definitionEn: a plant or animal brought in from elsewhere that harms local wildlife
items.example: An invasive species of crayfish is spreading through Polish rivers.

items.definitionEn: a plant or animal that naturally belongs in a particular place
items.example: Gardeners are encouraged to plant native species that support insects.

items.definitionEn: the complete disappearance of a species from the Earth
items.example: Hunting and habitat loss drove the species to extinction.

items.definitionEn: at extremely high risk of extinction in the wild
items.example: The species is listed as critically endangered on the international Red List.

items.definitionEn: a place where animals regularly gather to produce young
items.example: The lagoon is a breeding ground for seals in spring.

items.definitionEn: a strip of habitat that lets animals move safely between areas
items.example: A motorway without a wildlife corridor can split a forest population in two.

items.definitionEn: the destruction of the natural places where species live
items.example: Habitat loss is now a greater threat to wildlife than hunting.

items.definitionEn: the splitting of a habitat into smaller, isolated pieces
items.example: Roads cause habitat fragmentation that isolates animal populations.

items.definitionEn: catching so many fish that stocks cannot recover
items.example: Overfishing has emptied some North Sea stocks of cod.

items.definitionEn: the illegal hunting or catching of wild animals
items.example: Rangers risk their lives to stop poaching of elephants for ivory.

items.definitionEn: the illegal trade in wild animals or their body parts
items.example: Wildlife trafficking is a serious organised crime as well as a conservation issue.

items.definitionEn: breeding endangered animals in zoos or centres to save the species
items.example: Captive breeding brought the European bison back from the brink.

items.definitionEn: colouring or shape that helps an animal hide in its surroundings
items.example: The moth's camouflage makes it almost invisible on tree bark.

items.definitionEn: a feature that helps a living thing survive in its environment
items.example: Thick fur is an adaptation to life in a cold climate.

items.definitionEn: a long, deep sleep through winter to save energy
items.example: Hedgehogs survive the cold months through hibernation.

items.definitionEn: the regular, long-distance movement of animals, usually seasonally
items.example: The autumn migration of storks is a familiar sight in Polish villages.

items.definitionEn: the plants growing in a particular area
items.example: Fire destroyed the vegetation on the hillside, leaving bare soil.

items.definitionEn: a forest of trees that shed their leaves in autumn
items.example: A deciduous forest lets more light reach the ground in spring.

items.definitionEn: a plant that keeps its leaves all year
items.example: Pine is evergreen, so the forest stays green even in January.

items.definitionEn: an organism that breaks down dead plants and animals
items.example: Fungi act as a decomposer and return nutrients to the soil.

items.definitionEn: variety in the genes of a species, which helps it survive change
items.example: A tiny population has little genetic diversity and is vulnerable to disease.

items.definitionEn: a sudden, violent shaking of the ground
items.example: The earthquake brought down buildings that had not been reinforced.

items.definitionEn: water covering land that is normally dry
items.example: After days of rain the river burst its banks and caused a flood.

items.definitionPl: pożar lasu / pożar w terenie otwartym
items.definitionEn: a large, uncontrolled fire in countryside or forest
items.example: A wildfire spread through the dry pine forest in hours.

items.definitionEn: a sudden fall of rock or earth down a slope
items.example: Heavy rain triggered a landslide that blocked the mountain road.

items.definitionEn: a large mass of snow falling rapidly down a mountain
items.example: Skiers were warned not to leave the marked routes because of avalanche risk.

items.definitionEn: a huge sea wave caused by an underwater earthquake or eruption
items.example: Coastal towns had only minutes to flee after the tsunami warning.

items.definitionEn: when a volcano throws out lava, ash and gas
items.example: Ash from the volcanic eruption closed airports across the region.

items.definitionEn: a very powerful tropical storm with extremely strong winds
items.example: A hurricane tore roofs off houses along the coast.

items.definitionEn: a violent, spinning column of air that touches the ground
items.example: The tornado flattened barns in a narrow strip across the fields.

items.definitionEn: a large, rotating storm system, often over tropical seas
items.example: The cyclone brought destructive winds and a dangerous storm surge.

items.definitionEn: a smaller earthquake that follows a larger one
items.example: An aftershock overnight made residents afraid to sleep indoors.

items.definitionEn: the point on the Earth's surface above where an earthquake starts
items.example: The epicentre of the quake was just offshore.

items.definitionEn: a number that measures the strength of an earthquake
items.example: The quake had a magnitude of 6.2 and was felt in several countries.

items.definitionEn: earthquakes and other vibrations in the Earth's crust
items.example: Scientists recorded unusual seismic activity under the volcano.

items.definitionEn: a sudden flood after extremely heavy rain
items.example: A flash flood swept cars off the road in the narrow valley.

items.definitionEn: a rise in sea level driven onshore by a storm
items.example: The storm surge overtopped the sea wall and flooded the harbour.

items.definitionEn: a rapid flow of wet earth down a slope
items.example: Deforestation on the hillside made a mudslide more likely after rain.

items.definitionEn: a sudden natural event that causes serious damage and loss of life
items.example: The region is still recovering from last year's natural disaster.

items.definitionEn: to move people from a dangerous place to safety
items.example: The mayor ordered residents to evacuate before the river rose further.

items.definitionEn: technology and procedures that alert people before a disaster hits
items.example: An early-warning system gave the town twenty minutes to reach higher ground.

items.definitionEn: practical help given after a flood, quake or similar event
items.example: Charities flew in tents and drinking water as disaster relief.

items.definitionEn: walls, barriers and other structures built to keep floodwater out
items.example: The city invested in flood defences after two devastating winters.

items.definitionEn: an extreme shortage of food affecting a whole region
items.example: Crop failure and conflict together produced a famine.

items.definitionEn: a situation in which harvests are much smaller than expected
items.example: A crop failure after the drought pushed food prices sharply up.

items.definitionEn: the large-scale cutting down of forests
items.example: Deforestation in the Amazon is driven partly by cattle ranching.

items.definitionEn: harmful substances that make air, water or land dirty
items.example: Factory pollution has made the river unsafe for swimming.

items.definitionEn: processing used materials so they can be made into new products
items.example: The town raised its recycling rate by introducing doorstep collections.

items.definitionEn: a site where rubbish is buried in the ground
items.example: Most plastic packaging still ends up in landfill.

items.definitionEn: coal, oil and gas formed from ancient plants and animals
items.example: Burning fossil fuels is the main source of extra carbon dioxide.

items.definitionEn: power from sources that will not run out, such as wind or sun
items.example: The country aims to produce half its electricity from renewable energy.

items.definitionEn: using resources in a way that does not damage the future
items.example: True sustainability means living within the limits of the planet.

items.definitionEn: the protection of animals, plants and natural places
items.example: Marine conservation includes limits on fishing in coastal waters.

items.definitionEn: the release of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere
items.example: The factory cut its carbon emissions by switching to cleaner fuel.

items.definitionEn: gases produced by engines, especially in vehicles
items.example: Rush-hour exhaust fumes make the air quality in the centre unhealthy.

items.definitionEn: how clean or polluted the air is in a place
items.example: Schools close outdoor PE when air quality falls below a safe level.

items.definitionEn: the presence of harmful substances in water
items.example: Chemical water contamination forced the village to use bottled supplies.

items.definitionEn: unwanted material produced by factories and industry
items.example: Illegal dumping of industrial waste poisoned the stream.

items.definitionEn: rubbish that is poisonous and dangerous to living things
items.example: The old plant left barrels of toxic waste buried on the site.

items.definitionEn: waste water from homes and toilets
items.example: Untreated sewage was discharged into the sea after the storm.

items.definitionEn: the burning of waste at high temperatures
items.example: Incineration reduces the volume of rubbish but can release fumes.

items.definitionEn: plastic items designed to be thrown away after one use
items.example: The café no longer gives out single-use plastic cutlery.

items.definitionEn: able to be broken down naturally by bacteria or fungi
items.example: The packaging is biodegradable and should rot in compost within weeks.

items.definitionEn: turning kitchen and garden waste into soil improver
items.example: Composting food scraps cuts the amount of rubbish sent to landfill.

items.definitionEn: electricity generated from sunlight
items.example: The school roof now produces solar power for the sports hall.

items.definitionEn: a group of wind turbines that generate electricity
items.example: A new wind farm is planned off the Baltic coast.

items.definitionEn: electricity generated from moving water
items.example: The dam produces hydropower but has changed the river's ecosystem.

items.definitionEn: heat from inside the Earth used to make power or warm buildings
items.example: Iceland uses geothermal energy to heat homes and swimming pools.

items.definitionEn: electricity produced by splitting atoms in a reactor
items.example: Supporters argue that nuclear power can cut carbon emissions quickly.

items.definitionEn: an accidental release of oil into the sea or onto land
items.example: The oil spill killed seabirds along fifty kilometres of coast.

items.definitionEn: extracting gas or oil by injecting liquid into rock at high pressure
items.example: Campaigners say fracking risks polluting groundwater.

items.definitionEn: allowing too many animals to feed on land, so plants cannot recover
items.example: Overgrazing left the hillside bare and prone to erosion.

items.definitionEn: economic progress that does not destroy the environment or future resources
items.example: Sustainable development tries to balance jobs with protection of nature.

items.definitionEn: designed to cause little harm to the environment
items.example: The shop switched to eco-friendly packaging made from recycled paper.

items.definitionEn: making a product or company look more environmentally friendly than it is
items.example: The advert was accused of greenwashing because the brand still relies on coal.

items.definitionEn: balancing the carbon you produce by saving the same amount elsewhere
items.example: The festival claims to be carbon-neutral after planting thousands of trees.

items.definitionEn: cutting emissions and offsetting the rest so the total is zero
items.example: The government pledged to reach net zero by 2050.

items.definitionEn: planting trees again where forest has been cut down
items.example: Reforestation of the valley began five years after the fire.

items.definitionEn: planting trees on land that was not recently forest
items.example: Afforestation of former farmland can store carbon but may reduce biodiversity if only one species is used.

items.definitionEn: restoring land so that natural processes and wildlife can return
items.example: Rewilding of the former airfield brought back wetlands and nesting birds.

items.definitionEn: an area of land protected for wildlife and habitats
items.example: Dogs must be kept on a lead in the nature reserve.

items.definitionEn: a part of the sea where fishing and other damage are limited
items.example: Trawling is banned inside the marine protected area.

items.definitionEn: a person who works to protect animals, plants and habitats
items.example: A conservationist spoke to the class about restoring peat bogs.

items.definitionEn: a person who campaigns to protect the natural environment
items.example: The environmentalist argued that new roads would fragment the forest.

items.definitionEn: the 2015 international treaty to limit global warming
items.example: Signatories to the Paris Agreement promised to cut greenhouse gases.

items.definitionEn: a powerful greenhouse gas produced by livestock, waste and leaks
items.example: Cattle farming is a major source of methane emissions.

items.definitionEn: using less energy to do the same job
items.example: Better insulation is a cheap way to improve energy efficiency at home.

items.definitionEn: illegally dumping rubbish in the countryside or on waste ground
items.example: Cameras were installed to catch fly-tipping on the forest track.

items.definitionEn: separating rubbish into types such as paper, glass and bio-waste
items.example: Waste sorting at home only works if collection lorries keep the streams separate.

items.definitionEn: an economic model that reuses and recycles instead of throwing away
items.example: A circular economy treats yesterday's packaging as tomorrow's raw material.

items.definitionEn: materials that will eventually run out
items.example: Oil and gas are finite resources, unlike wind and sunlight.

items.definitionEn: to reduce something until little remains
items.example: Intensive fishing can deplete stocks faster than they can recover.

items.definitionEn: a serious shortage of fresh water
items.example: Water scarcity already forces some cities to ration supplies in summer.

items.definitionEn: a chemical used to kill insects that damage crops
items.example: Overuse of pesticide is one reason bee numbers have fallen.

items.definitionEn: a substance added to soil to help plants grow
items.example: Rain washed fertiliser from the fields into the lake, causing algal blooms.

items.definitionEn: producing as much food as possible from the land, often with chemicals
items.example: Intensive farming can exhaust the soil if fields are never left to rest.

items.definitionEn: growing food without most synthetic chemicals
items.example: Organic farming usually yields less but can support more wildlife.

items.definitionEn: growing only one crop over a large area
items.example: Monoculture of maize leaves fields vulnerable to a single pest.

items.definitionEn: the decline in soil quality so that it grows less food
items.example: Soil degradation is a hidden threat to long-term food security.

items.definitionEn: supplying water to land so that crops can grow
items.example: Irrigation from the river has turned dry plains into farmland.

items.definitionEn: tiny pieces of plastic that pollute soil, water and living things
items.example: Fish in the lagoon now contain microplastics in their stomachs.

items.definitionEn: the sea becoming more acidic as it absorbs extra carbon dioxide
items.example: Ocean acidification makes it harder for shellfish to build their shells.

items.definitionEn: corals turning white and often dying when seas become too warm
items.example: A marine heatwave caused coral bleaching across the reef.

items.definitionEn: cutting down trees in breach of the law
items.example: Satellite images are used to detect illegal logging in remote forests.

items.definitionEn: clearing land by cutting and burning vegetation, often for farming
items.example: Slash-and-burn agriculture is still used to clear rainforest for crops.
